inverse-determinant-s2.title: A parallelogram
inverse-determinant-s2.text: A parallelogram has one corner at the origin and two sides along the vectors from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 1)$ and from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 3)$.

mistakes.why: Subtract the off-diagonal product: $ad - bc = 8 - 6$, not $8 + 6$.

options: Both, since neither is the identity
Neither, since no entry is zero

why.correct: $\det B = 6(2) - 3(4) = 12 - 12 = 0$, so $B$ has no inverse. $\det A = 2 \ne 0$, so $A$ does.
options: A nonzero determinant means $A$ is invertible.
A matrix need not be $I$ to have an inverse; it needs a nonzero determinant.
Nonzero entries do not guarantee an inverse; $\det B = 0$.

why.correct: Swap the diagonal, negate the others, divide by $\det A = 2$: $\frac{1}{2}\left[ \begin{matrix} 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -1 & 2 \end{matrix} \right]$.
options: Reciprocals of the entries do not undo matrix multiplication.
Change the signs of the off-diagonal entries.
This is the right side; multiply it by $A^{-1}$.
Use $A^{-1}$; dividing $7$ by entries of $A$ does not solve the system.

items.q: Which fact shows that no matrix can undo multiplication by $B$?

why.correct: $B\left[ \begin{matrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right]$. Two different columns give the same product, so an undo matrix would have to send $\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right]$ back to both at once.
options: Two inputs, one output: nothing can undo that.
Every matrix changes most inputs; an inverse can still change them back.
Size does not matter; $\det B = 0$ does.
Two different matrices giving different products is normal; it says nothing about undoing $B$.

items.q: What is the area of the parallelogram?

mistakes.why: $20$ is the $5 \times 4$ rectangle around it, which includes four corner triangles.

why.correct: The sides are $\left\langle 4, 1 \right\rangle$ and $\left\langle 1, 3 \right\rangle$, so the area is $\left| \det \left[ \begin{matrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{matrix} \right] \right| = \left| 12 - 1 \right| = 11$.

items.q: Which matrix has the two sides as its columns?

options: $(5, 4)$ is the far corner, not a side from the origin.
Each column is upside down: the $x$-component goes on top.
This mixes the components of the two sides.

items.q: The side from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 1)$ is doubled to go to $(8, 2)$; the other side stays. What is the new area?

mistakes.why: Only one column doubled, so the area doubles once: $8(3) - 1(2) = 22$.
A longer side makes a larger parallelogram: $8(3) - 1(2) = 22$.

why.correct: $\det \left[ \begin{matrix} 8 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{matrix} \right] = 24 - 2 = 22$: doubling one column doubles the area.

items.q: The two columns of the matrix are written in the other order. What happens?
options: The determinant becomes $-11$; the area stays $11$
The determinant and the area both stay $11$
The determinant becomes $0$, since the columns repeat

why.correct: $\det \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 \end{matrix} \right] = 1 - 12 = -11$. Swapping columns flips the sign, while the parallelogram, and its area $\left| -11 \right| = 11$, is the same.
options: Sign flips, area is the absolute value.
An area is never negative; it is $\left| \det \right|$.
The columns are still different vectors, so the determinant is not $0$.

items.q: Write $\det \left[ \begin{matrix} k & 3 \\ 2 & k \end{matrix} \right]$ as an expression in $k$.

mistakes.why: Subtract the other diagonal: $ad - bc = k^2 - 6$.
The order is $ad - bc$: main diagonal first.

items.q: For which positive $k$ does $\left[ \begin{matrix} k & 3 \\ 2 & k \end{matrix} \right]$ have no inverse?

why.correct: No inverse exactly when $\det = k^2 - 6 = 0$, so $k = \sqrt{6}$ (or $-\sqrt{6}$).

items.q: What is the determinant of $\left[ \begin{matrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{matrix} \right]$?

why.correct: Main diagonal product minus the other diagonal product.
$\det = 6 - 5 = 1$. Swap $2$ and $3$, negate $1$ and $5$, divide by $1$.
options: Swap the diagonal, negate the rest, divide by $1$.

items.q: Which matrices have inverses? Select all that apply.

why.correct: A matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not $0$.
options: $4 - 4 = 0$: the second column is twice the first.

items.q: A $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has $\det A = 2$. What is $\det(3A)$?

mistakes.why: $3A$ multiplies both columns by $3$, so the area grows by $3 \cdot 3 = 9$, not $3$.

why.correct: Both columns are tripled, so the parallelogram's area is multiplied by $3 \cdot 3 = 9$: $\det(3A) = 9 \cdot 2 = 18$.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix in order.
options: Compute the determinant $ad - bc$ and check it is not $0$
Change the signs of the two off-diagonal entries
Divide each entry by the determinant

why.correct: Determinant first (if it is $0$, stop: no inverse), then swap, negate, divide. Check by multiplying to get $I$.
